reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / AASLD
clinicalPearls: A benign, inherited disorder of predominantly conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with an otherwise normal liver profile and normal life expectancy
Caused by autosomal recessive loss of the hepatic uptake transporters OATP1B1 and OATP1B3 (encoded by SLCO1B1 and SLCO1B3), impairing re-uptake of bilirubin conjugates
Unlike Dubin-Johnson syndrome, the liver appears histologically normal with no dark pigment deposition
Total urinary coproporphyrin excretion is markedly increased, with a relative rise in the coproporphyrin I isomer, distinguishing it from the isolated isomer shift of Dubin-Johnson syndrome
Patients are typically asymptomatic apart from mild jaundice and require no specific treatment
On older oral cholecystography the gallbladder was visualised, in contrast to non-visualisation in Dubin-Johnson syndrome, a historically useful distinguishing feature
The main task is to recognise the disorder as benign and avoid unnecessary investigation
Because the defect impairs hepatic uptake of certain drugs handled by these transporters, altered handling of some medications can occur
reference.pathophysiology: Rotor syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by the combined deficiency of two hepatic sinusoidal uptake transporters, OATP1B1 and OATP1B3, encoded by SLCO1B1 and SLCO1B3. These transporters normally reclaim conjugated bilirubin that has refluxed from hepatocytes back into the bloodstream. When both are absent, conjugated bilirubin that escapes into plasma is not efficiently taken back up by the liver, producing a chronic, mainly conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with bilirubinuria. Because bilirubin conjugation and canalicular secretion are otherwise intact and there is no toxic accumulation, the liver histology is normal without the pigment seen in Dubin-Johnson syndrome. The disorder is benign and non-progressive; the affected transporters also mediate hepatic uptake of various drugs, which can alter their disposition.
additionalInvestigations: Fractionated serum bilirubin confirming a conjugated predominance
Total and fractionated urinary coproporphyrin showing markedly raised total excretion
Liver function tests confirming otherwise normal biochemistry
Imaging to exclude biliary obstruction where warranted
Genetic testing for SLCO1B1 and SLCO1B3 mutations
Liver biopsy only if needed, showing normal histology without pigment
redFlags: Atypical features such as raised alkaline phosphatase, abnormal aminotransferases, or pruritus prompting evaluation for another disorder
New jaundice with systemic illness suggesting a superimposed hepatobiliary process
Unexplained progressive jaundice inconsistent with a benign course
reference.prognosis: Rotor syndrome is entirely benign with normal life expectancy and no progression to chronic liver disease; no treatment is required beyond reassurance and awareness of altered handling of drugs dependent on the affected transporters.
pitfalls: Pursuing extensive or invasive investigation for a harmless condition
Failing to distinguish it from Dubin-Johnson syndrome using coproporphyrin patterns
Overlooking altered pharmacokinetics of drugs handled by OATP transporters
Assuming all subsequent jaundice is due to the syndrome without excluding new pathology
